verses.translation_literal: Of David. Contend, YHWH, [with] my contenders; fight [with] my fighters.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song of David. Take up my quarrel, LORD. Stand against the ones who stand against me; make war on the ones who make war on me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm opens with courtroom and battlefield in one breath. The root ריב means to bring a lawsuit, to argue a case before a judge; לחם means to fight with weapons. David asks God to do both: be his advocate and be his general. The Hebrew says it with a mirror shape: 'contend, O YHWH, with my contenders; fight with my fighters.' Each verb returns as a noun, so the enemy is named by what he does, and God is asked to do it back to him. Direct this as a plea said fast, almost under the breath, by a man who has run out of other options.

The KJV 'plead my cause ... with them that strive with me' keeps the legal flavour in the first half but loses the repetition of the root, and 'fight against them that fight against me' adds 'against', which the Hebrew does not have (it uses the marker אֶת, 'with'). The marker is ambiguous in itself: 'fight with' can mean alongside or against, and context decides. Verse numbering: the Hebrew counts the superscription 'Of David' as verse 1, which is why the KJV has it as verse 0.

philological_notes.note: Imperative of 'to contend, to bring a case'. Used both of lawsuit and of quarrel. The next noun יְרִיבַי, 'my contenders', repeats the root, so the enemy is defined as the one who is in a dispute with David.
Imperative 'fight', with the same root in the noun לֹחֲמָי, 'my fighters'. Rashi notes that the word comes from 'war' (milchamah).
The superscription with the preposition lamed, usually read as 'of/by David' (authorship), though the tradition takes it to place the psalm in his life; Radak attaches it to the flight from Saul.

verses.translation_literal: Take hold [of] shield and body-shield, and rise for my help.
verses.translation_dramatic: Take up the shield, the great shield and the small. Get up, LORD, and come to my help.
verses.directors_commentary:
A war god is being asked to arm. Two shields: the מָגֵן, the small round buckler carried on the arm, and the צִנָּה, the large body shield, tall enough to hide a man (carried before the soldier, as with Goliath's shield-bearer). In the ancient world a king's god went to battle and the army fought under his banner; David asks YHWH to put on the gear himself. The commentators, including Radak and Metzudat David, say plainly that this is a figure, 'like a man holding weapons', and the verb חָזַק, 'seize firmly', means taking hold with strength. Say the line with the movement of a man standing up from the table.

The KJV's 'stand up for mine help' is an archaism that hides the Hebrew idiom: the verb is simply 'rise', and the preposition 'in/for my help' is a bet of aid. 'Buckler' in the KJV and ASV is a fair equivalent for צִנָּה, though the Hebrew word is the larger shield. BBE 'Be a breastplate to me' drops the image.

philological_notes.note: Two kinds of shield, small and large; Metzudat Zion calls them 'names of weapons for protection'. The pair appears elsewhere as a fixed phrase for full armour.
'Seize firmly, take hold'; Radak compares Genesis 21:18 ('hold him in your hand'). The picture is of God as a warrior taking weapons in his hand.

verses.translation_literal: And draw out spear and close off [the way] to meet my pursuers. Say to my soul: I [am] your salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: Draw the spear. Bar the road in the faces of the ones who hunt me down. And then say to my soul, quietly, so that I can hear it: I am your rescue.
verses.directors_commentary:
The picture moves from arming to the fight itself. הָרֵק means to empty out, to unsheathe, the same verb used of drawing a sword in Exodus 15:9 (Rashi cites it) and of Abraham's 'drawing out' his trained men in Genesis 14:14. The spear is unsheathed, and then comes a word that is one of the hardest in the psalm: סְגֹר. Rashi and Ibn Ezra take it as 'shut', block the way so the pursuers cannot get through; Radak records the other view, that it names another weapon. The KJV 'stop the way' goes with the first and adds 'also' for a vav that means only 'and'.

The last line is the point of the verse and the key for the actor: it is not asked of the enemy but of God's own voice. David wants to hear, inside himself, the words 'I am your salvation'. The Hebrew נֶפֶשׁ, 'throat, life, self', is the same word that the enemies are after in verse 4: they seek the soul to take, he asks that the soul be spoken to. The KJV translates as 'soul' and loses the physical image of a throat under threat. Radak reads the line as a word to put courage in the heart, against the fear described in Leviticus 26:36.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil imperative: 'to empty out', so 'to draw (a weapon)'. Rashi compares Exodus 15:9 and Genesis 14:14; Radak compares Ezekiel 5:12.

Either imperative 'close' (block the road, Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David) or the name of a weapon (Radak mentions this view, with Meiri). Not settled; the context favours the first reading as parallel to the spear.
'Your salvation', with a feminine singular suffix: 'soul' (nefesh) is grammatically feminine, so the one addressed is the soul. Radak says the word is meant to put strength in the heart.

verses.translation_literal: May they be ashamed and humiliated, [those who] seek my soul. May they be turned back backward and abashed, [those who] devise my harm.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them be shamed, let them be brought low, the ones who hunt for my life. Let them be turned around and sent back the way they came, red-faced, the ones who sit planning my ruin.
verses.directors_commentary:
The first of many curses in the psalm, and note that they are mostly wishes about shame, not about killing. In a culture of honour, to be 'ashamed and humiliated' is a public defeat: your plan fails in front of everyone. The four verbs are two pairs: בּוֹשׁ and כָּלַם, 'shame' and 'disgrace', then סוּג, 'turned back', and חָפֵר, 'blush, be abashed'. The enemies are named by two participles that stand in parallel to the fighters of verse 1: those who 'seek my soul', i.e. hunt for my life, and those who 'devise my harm', i.e. sit and plan. Malbim says the second group are the lighter, those who only plan.

The KJV 'confounded' and 'brought to confusion' for כָּלַם and חָפֵר are old English for being thrown into disorder; the Hebrew is about shame. KJV also renders נַפְשִׁי as 'soul' where 'life' is meant, and 'devise my hurt' is right. 'Turned back' is a battle image: the pursuers' charge is broken (Radak compares Psalm 44:19, 'our heart has not turned back').

philological_notes.note: 'May they be turned back backward': the verb and its adverb say the same thing twice. A military term for a retreat. Radak ties it to Psalm 44:19.
'Seekers of my soul': nefesh is both the throat and the life, so the enemies are hunting for my life. Radak links this with the soul addressed in verse 3.

verses.translation_literal: May they be like chaff before [the] wind, and [the] angel of YHWH pushing.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them be chaff in front of the wind, with the angel of the LORD behind them, shoving.
verses.directors_commentary:
The image comes from the threshing floor. After the grain is trampled, the farmer tosses it into the evening breeze: the heavy kernels drop, the מֹץ, the husk, the light waste, is carried off. Chaff is the standard biblical picture of what has no weight and no future (Psalm 1:4). The new touch is the messenger: מַלְאַךְ יְהוָה, here a warrior who pushes. Radak and Ibn Ezra make the point that chaff blown by wind sometimes catches on a fence and stays, but chaff driven by an angel never settles. Play the angel as unseen pressure, not a figure on stage.

The KJV 'chase' is a slight confusion: the Hebrew דּוֹחֶה, 'thrusting, shoving away', is a different verb from the 'pursue' of verse 6, and the KJV makes them nearly the same. ASV 'driving them on' is closer. BBE 'dust from the grain' is a gloss for 'chaff'. Also note 'angel' is the same Hebrew word as 'messenger': a malak is first an envoy, then a heavenly being.

philological_notes.note: Chaff, the husks blown off in winnowing. Radak calls it fine straw that drifts before the wind; Metzudat Zion calls it the waste of the grain.
Participle 'thrusting, pushing aside'. The point, in Radak's reading, is that unlike a wind, the angel allows no resting place.

verses.translation_literal: May their way be darkness and slippery places, and [the] angel of YHWH pursuing them.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let their road be dark and slick with falling, and let the angel of the LORD be right behind them, running them down.
verses.directors_commentary:
The curse now turns to the ground under their feet. Two hazards: חֹשֶׁךְ, darkness, and חֲלַקְלַקּוֹת, 'slippery places', a doubled form (the root חלק, smooth, said twice) that sounds like feet skidding: cha-lak-la-kot. Ibn Ezra notes the doubling, and Rashi cites Jeremiah 23:12, 'their way shall be to them as slippery places in the gloom; they shall be driven on and fall'. Rashi explains that the darkness stops them from watching out for the slippery places. Radak adds the logic of the third element: a man in the dark, on slick ground, can still walk slowly and perhaps survive, but if someone is chasing him, he must run, and then he falls.

The KJV 'dark and slippery' turns two nouns into adjectives and softens the noun 'slippery places'; and 'persecute' for רָדַף is a theological word where Hebrew means plain 'chase, pursue' (cf. v.3 where KJV also said 'persecute', Webster too). Keep it physical: an actual chase, at night, on wet stone.

philological_notes.note: 'Slippery places', a reduplicated plural from the root for smooth. Ibn Ezra compares the doubled form with sacharchar, 'swarthy'; Rashi cites Jeremiah 23:12.
'Pursuing them': the same root as 'my pursuers' in verse 3. The pursued are now the pursuers' target. The KJV 'persecute' is too narrow.

verses.translation_literal: For without cause they hid for me [the] pit of their net; without cause they dug for my soul.
verses.translation_dramatic: For nothing, for no reason at all, they hid their net for me, pit and all. For nothing they dug it, a hole for my life.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the psalm gives its reason. The key word is חִנָּם, 'for nothing, without cause', and it comes twice, at the start of each half, so that the accusation rings like a bell: for nothing, for nothing. In the ancient world a lawsuit or a vendetta needed grounds; David claims there were none. Radak adds that there may be a reading 'without violence in my hands', i.e. I have done no wrong.

The image is a hunter's trap. Radak describes how hunters dig a pit in a field, cover it over with nets and earth, and the animal falls in. The Hebrew phrase שַׁחַת רִשְׁתָּם, 'pit of their net', packs both into one chain, and commentators disagree on how it should be read: a pit with a net over it, or 'pit' and 'net' as two traps. The KJV 'their net in a pit' chooses one reading and drops the second חִנָּם's place in the sentence by turning the clause into a relative ('which without cause they have digged'). The Hebrew has no 'which'. The verb חָפַר also gives us the sound-play with verse 4's יַחְפְּרוּ, 'be abashed': same consonants, ironic echo, the diggers will blush.

philological_notes.note: 'For nothing, gratis, without cause': from the root of 'favour' (chen), something given or done for no reason. The word is placed twice for emphasis. Radak and Metzudat David read it as 'with no violence in my hands'.

Literally 'pit of their net'. Radak explains this as a hunting pit hidden under a net; Metzudat Zion and Meiri allow reading them as two separate things. Radak also notes a rabbinic usage that treats the word as a variant of another meaning.

verses.translation_literal: May ruin come to him, [which] he does not know, and his net which he hid, may it catch him; in ruin may he fall in it.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let ruin come down on him, and let him never see it coming. Let the net he hid be the net that closes on him, and let him fall into the very ruin he made.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the curse mirrors the crime. The enemy buried his trap in secret; let ruin arrive in secret too: שׁוֹאָה לֹא־יֵדָע, a disaster 'he does not know'. The Hebrew uses the root of 'ruin' twice (שׁוֹאָה ... בְּשׁוֹאָה), and the net which he hid is the net that catches him: a classic measure-for-measure ending, found throughout Psalms (compare Psalm 7:16). Rashi describes how a net is hidden under straw or earth so that the passer-by does not notice it; Radak says the ruin is like sudden panic, as in Proverbs 3:25.

A grammar point to play: the verbs are singular ('him', 'his net') although the enemies of the earlier verses were plural. Radak reads this as each enemy singly, or perhaps Saul. The KJV preserves the singular. The word שׁוֹאָה is 'sudden devastation, storm'; Rashi and Metzudat David read it instead as 'darkness' (compare Job 30:3), which would tie it to verse 6. KJV 'at unawares' paraphrases 'he does not know'; the Hebrew has simply 'which he does not know'.

philological_notes.note: Sudden ruin, devastation; used elsewhere of a storm that comes without warning. Rashi and Metzudat Zion read it as 'darkness', citing Job 30:3. Radak compares Proverbs 3:25.
'May it catch him': the net is feminine, so the verb is feminine. The verb 'to capture' normally describes taking a city or an animal.

verses.translation_literal: And my soul will rejoice in YHWH; it will exult in his salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I, all of me, will sing in the LORD. I will leap for joy at his rescue.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the long curse the music changes. 'And my soul' is the same nefesh that the enemies sought (v.4) and that God was asked to speak to (v.3); now it is the soul that speaks. Two verbs of joy in parallel, גִּיל and שׂוּשׂ, both words of physical gladness: to spin, to leap, to dance for joy. Rashi says it will be when I see their fall; Radak says when he takes vengeance and rescues my life from those who planned to take it. The Targum softens 'in the LORD' to 'in the word of the LORD', a habit of paraphrase.

The KJV 'shall be joyful ... shall rejoice' flattens two different verbs into near synonyms and turns plain futures into 'shall'. The Hebrew imperfect can mean 'will' or 'would that it might'. Play it as the exhale after the held breath of the first eight verses. Also note the shift of address: until now God was 'you'; here he is 'he' ('his salvation'), as the psalmist turns to speak about God to the congregation.

philological_notes.note: 'Rejoice, spin with joy': the root has the sense of circling, dancing. Often paired with שׂוּשׂ.
'My soul/self': Ibn Ezra reads it as the higher soul that is bound to the body.

verses.translation_literal: All my bones will say: YHWH, who [is] like you, delivering [the] poor from [one] stronger than he, and [the] poor and needy from his robber?
verses.translation_dramatic: Every bone in me will speak: LORD, who is like you? You pull the poor man out of the hands of the strong; you tear the poor and the needy away from the one who robs them.
verses.directors_commentary:
The bones talk. In Hebrew thought the bones are the frame of the body, the deepest part, and to say 'all my bones' is to say 'my whole being'. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as the body standing for the person; Radak adds that the verse is a pairing of soul and body, as in Psalm 84:3, 'my heart and my flesh sing for joy'. The speech is a hymn question, מִי כָמוֹךָ, 'who is like you?', the same phrase as the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:11), turned from a battle cry into a prayer of thanks. Direct the bones as a chorus.

The speaker puts himself in the category of the poor: עָנִי, 'poor, afflicted', and אֶבְיוֹן, 'needy, begging'. These are the people with no legal protection in a world where the strong can seize land or goods; God is their champion. The Hebrew has two names, 'poor' and 'poor-and-needy', for the victim, and two for the oppressor, 'one stronger than he' and 'his robber'. The KJV 'him that spoileth him' uses spoil in its old sense of rob; KJV 'too strong for him' is correct. Note that the word 'all' is pointed with a long vowel, a detail Radak and Meiri comment on.

philological_notes.note: 'My bones': standing for the body or the whole self. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as the body that bears witness; Radak mentions philosophical readings but says they do not fit the verse.
'Who is like you?': the language of the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15:11), here used for rescue of the poor, not victory over an army.
Pair of words for the poor: 'afflicted/humbled' and 'needy, desiring'. A fixed phrase for those without power.

verses.translation_literal: Witnesses of violence rise up; [that] which I do not know they ask me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Witnesses stand up, violent witnesses. They question me about things I have never known.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the courtroom of verse 1 comes into view. In Israelite law, a case was settled by witnesses standing up before the elders at the gate; a person was convicted on the testimony of two or three (Deuteronomy 19:15). עֵדֵי חָמָס, 'witnesses of violence', is a phrase for those who testify not to truth but to hurt. The word חָמָס is not 'false' but 'violent, lawless', the sin that filled the earth before the flood; the KJV 'false witnesses' interprets it as perjury, which is surely the sense here (compare Exodus 23:1, Deuteronomy 19:16) but the Hebrew names the harm, not the lie.

The second line is a cross-examination. יִשְׁאָלוּנִי, 'they ask me', is a legal interrogation: they demand answers, perhaps demand repayment, about matters David knows nothing of. The KJV 'laid to my charge' turns this into a formal accusation; BBE's 'put questions to me' is closer. Radak reads it as a demand for money on a false claim, but admits that Samuel does not record the episode; Malbim has the witnesses claiming, for example, that his father owed a sum. Treat the line as a scene: a man on the stand, answering for what he cannot even identify.

philological_notes.note: 'Witnesses of violence': perjurers who bring harm. Compare Exodus 23:1 and Deuteronomy 19:16 ('a witness of violence' against a man).
'They ask me': the verb of questioning, also of demanding something. Ibn Ezra and Radak read it as a demand to give what David does not have.

verses.translation_literal: They repay me evil in place of good, bereavement to my soul.
verses.translation_dramatic: Evil is what they pay me for good, and the price is a soul left bereaved.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the wound under the whole psalm: loyalty answered with betrayal. The language is of payment: שִׁלֵּם, 'to pay back, make whole', normally used for restitution, now turned upside down: they 'pay back' evil where good was due. The commercial idiom תַּחַת, 'in place of, in exchange for', makes it a bad bargain. The same lament appears in Psalm 109:5. Radak says that David had done these men good, and they repay him with a claim for money he never owed.

The last words, שְׁכוֹל לְנַפְשִׁי, 'bereavement to my soul', are the hardest to put in English. שְׁכוֹל is the loss of children, the state of a woman robbed of her sons; here it means a soul emptied out, stripped of everything. The KJV 'to the spoiling of my soul' is a mistranslation: 'spoiling' means plunder in older English, but the Hebrew means bereavement. ASV 'bereaving' has it right. Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion take it as death. Let the line fall away quietly after the sharper beat of the first half.

philological_notes.note: 'Bereavement, loss of children', and by extension a state of desolation. The KJV 'spoiling' does not follow the Hebrew. Metzudat Zion glosses it as death; Radak as taking by violence.
'Evil in place of good': a stock phrase for ingratitude. Metzudat David says 'in place of the good I did them'.

verses.translation_literal: And I—in their being sick, my clothing [was] sackcloth; I afflicted with the fast my soul; and my prayer upon my bosom returns.
verses.translation_dramatic: But I, when sickness laid them low, I put on sackcloth. I starved my own soul down to nothing, I fasted for them, and when I prayed, the prayer came home to me, falling back on my own breast.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalmist sets his own conduct against that of his enemies. When they were ill, he did what a loyal kinsman did: he put on sackcloth, the coarse goat-hair cloth of mourning, and fasted. The Hebrew idiom is "I afflicted my soul" (עִנֵּיתִי נַפְשִׁי), the standard ancient phrase for fasting, so the fast is a bodily and a religious act at once, a way of pleading with God for the sick person. KJV "humbled my soul with fasting" is faithful enough, but ASV's "afflicted" is closer to the physical sting. Note the definite article in בַצּוֹם, "with *the* fast": Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as the known fast day that a sick man's family and friends proclaimed, and the speaker joined them as if he were kin.

The last clause is the hard one. "My prayer returns upon my bosom" can mean that the prayer came back unanswered, that it was prayed with head bowed against the chest, or that if his prayer for them was a sham, may the blessing he asked for them fall on himself instead. Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David take the last view: he is heading off the charge that his mourning was a show. KJV "returned into mine own bosom" keeps the ambiguity but hides that the preposition is plain "upon" (עַל) and the verb is imperfect, a continuing "returns".

philological_notes.note: Literally "I afflicted my soul/throat/self": the set idiom for fasting, as in the Day of Atonement command. Ibn Ezra observes that every such affliction is tied to the fast.
"Upon my bosom it returns." Read as a wish that the prayer's good come back on the speaker (Radak, Rashi, Metzudat David), or as bowed prayer (R. Levi in Ibn Ezra).

verses.translation_literal: As a friend, as a brother to me, I went about; as a mourner of a mother, mourning, I bowed down.
verses.translation_dramatic: I walked among them as though each one were my friend, my brother. I went about in gloom, bent low, like a son behind his mother's bier.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two similes of grief. First, he behaved "as a friend, as a brother": the verb הִתְהַלַּכְתִּי is the reflexive "I went to and fro", the restless pacing of a worried man. KJV "I behaved myself as though he had been my friend" turns the plural enemies into a single "he" and softens a vivid pacing into manners; the Hebrew has no "he" and no "as though", only the bare "like a friend, like a brother".

Second, "as a mourner of a mother": the Hebrew says "mother", not father, and the commentators ask why. Radak answers that a person grieves most for the one who bore, nursed and fed him; Meiri adds that the mother's loss brings no consolation of inheritance. The two verbs, קֹדֵר ("darkened, in dark clothes", the root of Joel 2:10's darkening sun and moon, Metzudat Zion) and שַׁחוֹתִי ("I bowed low"), build a picture of a man in black, stooped to the ground. Rashi reads them as blackness and lowliness.

philological_notes.note: "Darkened, in mourning dress": the root of darkness, used of heavenly bodies in Joel 2:10 and of the dim, dirty look of a mourner. Radak notes it can describe the face or the black clothing.
"Mother", not father: Radak says one grieves most for the one who bore and fed one.

verses.translation_literal: And at my stumbling they rejoiced and they gathered; they gathered against me, the smitten, and I did not know; they tore and were not still.
verses.translation_dramatic: But when I stumbled, they were glad. They gathered, gathered against me, the broken ones, the smitten, and I never knew why. They tore at me and would not be still.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns at once. The same word that ended the last passage's mourning, "and I", gives way to "but at my stumbling". בְּצַלְעִי is "at my limping", the noun from the root of Jacob's limp (Genesis 32:32, as Metzudat Zion notes), so it means any fall, illness or reverse that makes a man lame. The enemies do not rush to help: they rejoice and gather. The doubled verb ("and they gathered, they gathered") makes a mob.

נֵכִים is uncertain. Rashi and Metzudat Zion take it as the lame, those struck in the feet; Radak takes it as the abject, the beaten-down (compare Job 30:8); Ibn Ezra says "smitten of spirit". KJV and ASV's "abjects" is archaic and guesses; BBE's "low persons" interprets; YLT's "smiters" reads it as active, which the form does not support. "The smitten" keeps the doubt.

The last clause, "they tore and were not still", is two bare verbs with no object. KJV supplies "me", which fixes a reading: "tear" may be flesh, garments or reputation, or may mean "opened (their mouths) wide" in laughter (Radak, Metzudat Zion), and דמם is "to be silent" (Ibn Ezra), not KJV's "ceased".

philological_notes.note: "The smitten": disputed. Lame in the feet (Rashi, Metzudat Zion), abject and beaten-down (Radak), or smitten in spirit (Ibn Ezra).
"They tore": flesh, cloth or reputation; or "opened wide" the mouth, as in Jeremiah 4:30 and 22:14 cited by Radak.

verses.translation_literal: With the godless, mockers of a cake, gnashing against me their teeth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Godless, mocking, laughing for a crumb of bread, they grind their teeth against me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The most obscure line of the psalm. The Hebrew is a chain of nouns in construct, "godless ones, mockers of a cake", and מָעוֹג is the problem. The word is otherwise only in 1 Kings 17:12, where the widow of Zarephath says she has no "cake" (מָעוֹג) of bread; Rashi and Metzudat Zion cite exactly that verse. Read so, these are men who jeer for a bit of food, paid mockers and hangers-on at a rich man's table; Rashi says they flatter Saul so that he will feed and water them. Radak knows another reading, "idle talk" (with a Talmudic parallel), and so does Ibn Ezra, who says the mockery is as sweet to them as food to eat.

KJV "hypocritical mockers in feasts" is a guess that turns "cake" into "feasts" and חָנֵף (godless, polluted) into "hypocritical". Radak adds that the preposition בְּ here means "with", as in Psalm 44:6, so the picture is the crowd joining the godless. The ending is physical and plain: "they gnash their teeth", the grinding of teeth in rage or glee (Lamentations 2:16, Radak).

philological_notes.note: "Cake": from עוּגָה, a round cake of bread. Only elsewhere in 1 Kings 17:12. Hence mockers for a piece of bread (Rashi), or a figure for gluttony or for idle talk (Radak).
"Gnash": grinding the teeth together in anger (Metzudat Zion) or glee at revenge (Radak, citing Lamentations 2:16).

verses.translation_literal: My Lord, how long will you look on? Bring back my soul from their ruins, from the young lions my only one.
verses.translation_dramatic: Lord, how long will you only watch? Bring my life back from their ruin, from the young lions, my one and only life.
verses.directors_commentary:
The shift from description to plea. "How long will you look?" is a bold question: the God who sees is accused, gently, of merely watching. Radak compares Job 21:17 ("how often"), and Rashi paraphrases it as "how much patience do you have, to look on all this?" The verb הָשִׁיבָה is "bring back", the word used for restoring from captivity, and so KJV "rescue" is a gloss; the speaker is already half-lost and wants his life brought back.

מִשֹּׁאֵיהֶם is difficult: the word is שׁוֹאָה's relative, "ruins", "storms" or "din". KJV "destructions" fits; Radak and Meiri hear "their roar and clamor", Rashi and Metzudat Zion "darkness". "Young lions" is the image of the enemies' teeth (Ibn Ezra), keeping the imagery of verse 16. KJV's "my darling" for יְחִידָתִי sounds like affection but means "my only one": the only life he has, glossed "my soul" by Radak (compare Psalm 22:20) and Metzudat Zion.

philological_notes.note: "My only one": the soul as the single, irreplaceable thing. Radak says it is simply "my soul", as in Psalm 22.
"From their ruins": read variously as destruction, roaring din (Radak, Meiri), or darkness (Rashi, Metzudat Zion). Ibn Ezra treats it as an unusual masculine plural for a feminine noun.

verses.translation_literal: I will give thanks to you in a great assembly; among a mighty people I will praise you.
verses.translation_dramatic: And I will thank you, in the great assembly, and praise you before a people numberless and strong.
verses.directors_commentary:
A vow. In the old world a rescued man paid his debt in public: thanksgiving was spoken before the congregation, with sacrifice, so that the whole assembly could witness what God had done. Ibn Ezra reads it as exactly that, a promise to thank God in the open once saved; Radak adds that the great assembly means all Israel together.

The verse is built on a parallel: the verb אוֹדְךָ (from ידה, "throw, confess, give thanks") and then אֲהַלֶּלְךָ (from הלל, the root of hallelujah). עָצוּם, "mighty", also means "numerous", as in Jeremiah 15:8 (Metzudat Zion). KJV "much people" is correct but old; the sense is a huge crowd, the opposite of the small, jeering mob of the last verses.

philological_notes.note: "Mighty" and also "numerous": Metzudat Zion cites Jeremiah 15:8 for the sense of multitude.

token_glosses.gloss: I will give thanks to you

verses.translation_literal: Let not rejoice over me my enemies [with] falsehood, those who hate me [for] nothing, [let them not] wink an eye.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not let them laugh over me, those who are my enemies and have no cause to be. Do not let them, those who hate me for nothing, trade their knowing glances, one eye narrowing to another across the crowd.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is still the prayer of a man who has just promised to thank the LORD before the great assembly, and it turns at once to the audience he fears: the people who are waiting for him to fall. Two crimes are named, and neither is a deed. One is rejoicing, the other is winking. In a shame-and-honor society, being laughed at by people who have no right to judge you is a wound on the whole household, and the psalmist asks that they be denied the pleasure.

The KJV smooths two things. 'Wrongfully rejoice' attaches שֶׁקֶר, 'falsehood', to the verb. The Hebrew sets it beside 'my enemies': they are enemies of falsehood, enemies without a true reason, as Rashi, Radak and Meiri all read it. And in 'neither let them wink with the eye that hate me', the KJV reverses the order and adds a 'with'. The Hebrew is blunter: 'those who hate me for nothing, an eye they pinch.' The negative אַל belongs to both halves (Metzudat David), so the second colon is still a prayer, not a report. Actors should play the wink as a small, silent act: the קָרַץ is the nip or pinch of the eyelid, a signal passed from one mocker to another (Radak, with Prov 6:13 and 16:30). It is cruelty that needs no words.

philological_notes.note: 'For nothing, without cause', from the word for favor or grace: something given gratis, and so something done with no reason. Here it is the enemies' hatred that has no cause. Radak glosses the neighboring שקר as 'for nothing' too, and ties it to 1 Sam 25:21.

To nip or pinch, here the eyelid: a wink of mockery or conspiracy. The same root is used for the lips and eyes of the scoundrel in Proverbs. Radak and Metzudat Zion describe it as a movement of the eyes in mockery.

verses.translation_literal: For not peace do they speak, and against the quiet of the land words of deceit they devise.
verses.translation_dramatic: For they never speak of peace. Against the quiet people of the land they sit and devise their deceitful words.
verses.directors_commentary:
"They do not speak shalom": in the ancient world, a greeting or a word of peace was the sign of a decent neighbor, and Radak compares Genesis 37:4, where Joseph's brothers "could not speak peaceably" to him. The enemies' mouths have no peace in them.

רִגְעֵי־אֶרֶץ, "the quiet of the land", is disputed. Radak takes it as "the meek, the gentle" (from a root meaning rest); Rashi, citing Dunash, "the crushed of the land"; Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion take it as "clefts" (as in Job 7:5), that is, hidden places where the plot is laid. KJV "them that are quiet in the land" follows the first view. Note that the verb יַחֲשֹׁבוּן, "they devise", is the same word used for craftsmen's designs: the lies are planned, not blurted.

philological_notes.note: "The quiet of the land": the meek (Radak), the crushed (Rashi), or hidden clefts (Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David, Metzudat Zion). Radak argues against the third.

verses.translation_literal: And they opened wide against me their mouth; they said, Aha, aha, our eyes, it has seen.
verses.translation_dramatic: And now their mouths gape wide against me. They say it, and they crow it twice: Aha! Aha! Our eyes have seen it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The winks of verse 19 have grown into open noise. The verb וַיַּרְחִיבוּ means to make broad, and what is broadened is the mouth, 'their mouth', a single mouth for the whole crowd: a gape of laughter, as Radak and Metzudat David take it, and perhaps also of appetite. Elsewhere Hebrew uses an open mouth for hunger and for the grave, and the sound here fits that. Then come the two syllables the KJV gives as 'Aha, aha'. הֶאָח is not a word but a shout, spat out twice, a cry of triumph over someone else's ruin (Rashi, Meiri, and Ezek 26:2, where Tyre says it of Jerusalem). Say it like a laugh with teeth in it.

The last clause is easy to flatten. The Hebrew has 'our eyes', in the dual, and the verb after it is feminine singular: 'our eyes, it has seen'. The KJV and ASV make it 'our eye hath seen it', singular and with an object added; BBE has 'our eyes have seen it', plural but also with 'it'. Hebrew gives no object. The crowd does not say what it saw, because it does not need to: it has seen what it wanted, as Radak and Metzudat David put it ('what we desired to see'), and the psalm leaves the reader to fill in the fall. Seeing the enemy's defeat with one's own eyes is a recurring wish in the Psalms (Ps 54:9, which Radak cites).

philological_notes.note: An interjection of gloating, here doubled for emphasis. Rashi, Meiri and Metzudat Zion all call it a word of joy, and Radak says the doubling shows the greatness of the joy. The same cry in Ezek 26:2 is Tyre's over fallen Jerusalem.
Hiphil of 'be wide': they made their mouth wide. The target is 'against me' (עלי), so the gape is hostile. Radak reads it as wide in laughter and in speech.
A feminine singular verb with a dual-form noun and a first-person-plural suffix. This is ordinary Hebrew agreement and not a defect. There is no object: the verb is bare, 'it has seen'.

verses.translation_literal: You have seen, YHWH; do not be silent. My Lord, do not be far from me.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have seen it, LORD. Do not keep silent. My Lord, do not stand far away from me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The answer to the mob. They said "our eye has seen"; the psalmist says "You have seen" (רָאִיתָה), and Ibn Ezra notes the match: "you have seen" against "our eye has seen", "do not be silent" against "they said". God's eye is set against theirs, God's voice against theirs.

The verb תֶּחֱרַשׁ is "be silent" (compare חֵרֵשׁ, deaf): Radak, "do not act as though deaf". The prayer uses both names, "YHWH" then "my Lord". KJV "This thou hast seen" adds "this"; the Hebrew has only the bare verb. Note too the pair of negatives: silence and distance, the two ways God might appear to abandon a petitioner.

philological_notes.note: "Do not be silent" (also "do not be deaf" in Radak's paraphrase). Set by Ibn Ezra against the enemies' "they said".

verses.translation_literal: Rouse yourself and wake up for my judgment, my God and my Lord, for my cause.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rise! Wake! Be stirred to my judgment, my God, my Lord, to my cause.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalmist now speaks as a litigant: מִשְׁפָּט (judgment, a legal decision) and רִיב (lawsuit, dispute) are courtroom words. In the ancient Near East the king or deity was the court of last appeal for those with no human patron, and the poor man's "cause" would be brought to him. The two imperatives, הָעִירָה and הָקִיצָה, are "be stirred" and "wake up". Both belong to sleeping: God is spoken of as if dozing while injustice passes. Radak says it is simply doubled speech for emphasis, "do not be as one asleep any more", with the added argument that God is both "my God" (no other judge) and "my Lord" (a master who defends his servant).

KJV "stir up thyself" is fine, though "even unto my cause" smooths a parallel that is really "for my judgment ... for my cause". Rashi, citing the Talmud, reads it as the heavenly court being roused. Malbim's own reading, that the dead witnesses the enemies named are being woken, is a flourish of his own.

philological_notes.note: "Rouse, awake": the imagery of a sleeping God, a standard way of asking for intervention. Radak reads the doubling as emphasis.
"My lawsuit, my cause": a legal term for a dispute brought to a judge.

verses.translation_literal: Judge me according to your righteousness, YHWH my God, and let them not rejoice over me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Judge me by your own righteousness, LORD my God, and let them not gloat over me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The petition closes the section. שָׁפְטֵנִי is "judge me" in the sense of "decide my case in my favor", "vindicate me"; Ibn Ezra, "take for me a just judgment from them". KJV "judge me" is literally right, but a modern reader hears condemnation; the speaker means to be declared in the right. The standard is not his own deeds but God's צֶדֶק, "righteousness": Metzudat David says "by the measure of your righteousness and not by my deeds", and Meiri adds mercy.

The verse ends where verse 19 began, with the same "let them not rejoice over me" (וְאַל־יִשְׂמְחוּ־לִי), the plea that frames the whole movement of verses 19 to 24, laughter against laughter.

philological_notes.note: "Judge me" meaning "vindicate me": take my case and rule for me. Ibn Ezra: "take for me a just judgment from them".
"According to your righteousness": God's own standard, not the speaker's merit (Metzudat David).

verses.translation_literal: Let them not say in their heart: Aha! Our desire! Let them not say: We have swallowed him up!
verses.translation_dramatic: Do not let them say it, not even in the dark of their own hearts, that little cry of glee: Aha! It is what we wanted! Do not let them say it aloud, either, that word they would smack their lips over: We have swallowed him whole!
verses.directors_commentary:
The speakers here are not on stage; the singer is quoting what he fears his enemies will say, and begging God to stop them before they can. Play it as a flinch. The word 'Aha' (he'ach) is a bark of triumph, the sound of someone who has watched a rival fall and is delighted; it is the same cry he heard in v.21, and the psalm now wants it silenced for good. The Hebrew asks that they not even say it 'in their heart', which Radak and Meiri both read as: let them not be able to rejoice even in secret.

The KJV's 'so would we have it' turns a single word into a sentence, and it blunts the shock. The Hebrew is simply nafsheinu, 'our nefesh'. Nefesh is the seat of appetite and also, literally, the throat, so 'our desire' sits right beside 'we have swallowed him', and the hungry mouth is the picture. 'Swallowed' (bala') is the language of Sheol and of the earth opening, of total, wordless destruction; the BBE's 'put an end to him' and the KJV's 'swallowed him up' both lose the plain bodily image of a gulp. Hearing it as the enemy's boast, an actor should savour the word.

philological_notes.note: An interjection of gloating, 'Aha!', not a word of joy but of malicious satisfaction. Its repetition in v.21 and v.25 frames the enemies' speech in this part of the psalm.
Literally 'our nefesh': throat, appetite, desire. The elliptical exclamation 'Our desire!' means 'Just what we wanted', and the throat sense prepares the verb 'swallowed'.
Piel, 'we have swallowed him': the intensive stem makes it a complete engulfing. Radak glosses it 'we have destroyed him'; Metzudat David specifies the object, David.

verses.translation_literal: Let them be ashamed and let them be abashed together, the rejoicers at my calamity; let them put on shame and disgrace, the ones who make themselves great over me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let shame find them, every one, and let them blush and stumble together, those who laughed when my ruin came. Let them dress themselves in shame, in disgrace, as in a coat, these men who swelled themselves up over me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The curse mirrors the crime. They gathered together to rejoice (v.15), so together they are to be ashamed; they gloated, so the word is 'let them put on' shame, the same verb as putting on a garment. In an honour-and-shame culture, to be publicly disgraced was a kind of social death, and the image is of a victim stripped and re-dressed in his enemy's disgrace. The doubling, ashamed and abashed, shame and disgrace, is the poetry's way of turning the volume up; Radak says it is repeated 'to strengthen'.

The KJV's 'mine hurt' softens ra'ah, which is the ordinary word for evil, calamity, disaster; these people are glad that the singer's life is going badly. 'Magnify themselves against me' is close, but the verb is the same gadal ('be great') that opens v.27 for God: the enemies make themselves big, and the psalm asks that God alone be made big. Metzudat David notes that each will see the shame of his neighbour, so the humiliation is shared out in public.

philological_notes.note: Two near-synonyms for being put to shame and confounded. Radak says the doubling is for emphasis.
'My calamity, my evil': the common word for disaster, which the KJV's 'hurt' understates. The people rejoice at the arrival of the trouble.

Hiphil of gadal, 'to make great'. With 'al, 'over me', it means to boast against, to exalt oneself at someone's expense; Radak ties it to the mouth, as in 'they opened wide their mouth against me' (v.21).

token_glosses.gloss: the ones who make themselves great

verses.translation_literal: Let them shout for joy and let them rejoice, those who desire my righteousness, and let them say continually: May YHWH be great, who desires the welfare of his servant.
verses.translation_dramatic: And let others sing out, let them rejoice, all who long to see me proved right. Let them say it without ceasing: Great is the LORD, who delights in the peace of his servant!
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns. After the shame of the gloaters comes the joy of the friends, and the whole psalm lifts. The verbs echo the gloaters' own: the enemies 'rejoiced' (same root, simeach) at the singer's calamity; now those who are on his side rejoice, and the rejoicing is the right kind. The word 'continually' (tamid) is the word for the daily temple offering, so the praise is meant to be steady, like a liturgy, not a single outburst.

The KJV 'favour my righteous cause' and ASV 'favor my righteous cause' import a legal sense that is only hinted: the Hebrew is 'those who desire my tsedek', 'my righteousness', which could be my vindication or simply what is right and due to me (Radak). The KJV's 'Let the Lord be magnified' is correct, and the point is the sound play: the enemies 'make themselves great' (magdilim, v.26) and the faithful say 'May YHWH be great' (yigdal); Ibn Ezra notices this contrast. 'Shalom' is not only peace but wholeness and wellbeing, the KJV's 'prosperity' being a bit narrow. 'His servant' is David for Radak, the whole people for Meiri.

philological_notes.note: 'Continually, perpetually'; the same word names the daily offering, so the praise is imagined as a standing liturgy.
'May YHWH be great': the answer to the enemies' self-magnifying (hamagdilim) in the previous verse. Ibn Ezra points to the contrast.
'The wellbeing of his servant': Radak says the servant is David; Meiri takes it to be Israel as a whole, comparing 'Jacob my servant'.

verses.translation_literal: And my tongue will murmur your righteousness, all the day your praise.
verses.translation_dramatic: And my own tongue will go on murmuring your justice, your praise, all the day long, until the day is gone.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends quietly, with one voice. The singer who began by calling for battle ends by promising to keep talking about God. Note the shift from 'they' to 'my tongue': Radak argues that if the others praise God, how much more should the singer's own tongue. Ibn Ezra hears an answer to the enemies' 'Aha' of v.25: their tongues spoke gloating, so now my tongue will speak of your righteousness.

The verb hagah is not 'speak' as the KJV has it but a low murmuring, the sound a person makes when meditating or reading aloud under the breath, the same verb as the one used of the blessed man in Psalm 1:2 who 'meditates' on the law day and night. 'All the day' is literal, 'the whole day', and the KJV's 'all the day long' is fine. 'Your righteousness' here is God's tsedek in answering the singer's plea and punishing the wicked (Malbim), and the word is the same that was 'my righteousness' in v.27: the singer's vindication is his God's righteousness, so praise is simply what vindication sounds like. Delivery: low, steady, with no performance left in it.

philological_notes.note: To murmur, mutter, utter in a low voice; in the Psalms, the sound of meditation. 'Speak' (KJV) is too loud; Metzudat Zion glosses it 'speak'.
'Your righteousness', God's own justice in acting for the singer. Malbim ties it to the punishment of the wicked, and 'your praise' to the reward of the righteous.
